title: How long should charter school contract terms be? https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/how-long-should-charter-school-contract-terms-be
author: Jeff Murray
source: The Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 24, 2026
summary: Jeff Murray reviews a National Association of Charter School Authorizers study of how authorizers in Colorado, Florida, Indiana, and Michigan decide how long to renew charter school contracts. Drawing on a survey of 39 authorizers and focus groups with 26 of them, the report finds five years to be the default, seen as long enough to gather data and give schools operational stability. Longer terms are rare rewards for sustained excellence that reduce paperwork and ease facility financing, but some schools declined after receiving them, leaving authorizers with fewer tools to intervene. Shorter terms are meant as leverage on struggling schools, yet respondents offered little evidence they work and noted they can accelerate staff turnover and enrollment decline. Murray notes that uniform five-year terms also create renewal clusters and erase quality signals. He endorses NACSA's recommendation that term length be set through a deliberate, performance-based process rather than by default, while acknowledging the small, nonrepresentative sample.
points: Five-year renewals dominate across the four states studied because they balance sufficient data with school stability.
Long-term renewals ease administrative burden and facility financing, but some schools declined in performance afterward with fewer intervention options available.
Short-term renewals are intended as leverage, yet authorizers reported little evidence they improve performance and noted harms to staffing, enrollment, and reputation.
NACSA warns that short renewals should never be used to postpone painful closure decisions, and urges policies that curb 'authorizer shopping'.
quotes: It is an authorizer’s job to determine whether schools are fulfilling the terms of their charters across numerous areas, not least of which is student outcomes. Contract renewal time is when those determinations matter most.
Respondents said that a five-year term provides them with enough data to make sound decisions and provides schools sufficient time to achieve any needed operational stability required by authorizers.
On the downside, however, respondents reported that some schools declined in performance after receiving long-term renewals, with fewer intervention tools then available to authorizers.

However, respondents provided little evidence that short-term renewals actually improved school performance. Repeated short-term renewals, respondents said, could also accelerate staff turnover, hasten enrollment declines, and do reputational harm to schools.

Having all or even most schools in a portfolio on similar terms creates clusters of renewals every year, resulting in a significant and ongoing administrative burden for authorizers that staggered/non-standard terms could alleviate.
To wit: The length of charter renewal terms should be determined through a deliberate, performance-based process, and not by default or tradition.
